preamble: A rhotic becoming the voiced dental fricative [ð] is rare but attested in two unrelated places. In Jèrriais, the Norman language of Jersey, /r/ between vowels and word-finally after a vowel developed into [ð], written 'th'. The change came after the 16th century, since Sercquiais, brought to Sark by Jersey settlers, does not have it; it is standard in the literary language and predominant in the western dialects, while the eastern dialects keep [ɾ]. In Woods Cree (the Cree 'th-dialect'), [ð] is the reflex of the Proto-Algonquian sonorant that Goddard reconstructs as *r (Bloomfield's *l), where other Cree dialects have y, n, l or r. Rocky (Missinipi) Cree, an r-dialect, has since changed its r to ð and merged with Woods Cree. The Outer Hebridean Scottish Gaelic realization of slender /ɾʲ/ as [ð] starts from a palatalized rhotic and is not included here.

examples.note: Plains Cree iyiniw, Swampy Cree ininiw, Moose Cree ililiw. Rocky (Missinipi) Cree historical r has also become ð, merging that dialect with Woods Cree.
Plains Cree kīya, Swampy Cree kīna, Moose Cree kīla.

sources: Starks, D., & Ballard, E. (2005). Woods Cree /ð/: An Unusual Type of Sonorant. International Journal of American Linguistics 71(1), 102-115. https://doi.org/10.1086/430580
